Excellencies, distinguished participants, colleagues, I hereby declare open the 49th meeting of the 61st session of the Human Rights Council. We will now turn to the urgent debate of today. As per usual practice, let me begin with a few practical details. On 23 of March, I received a letter from the Permanent Representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran to the United Nations Office in Geneva, on behalf of the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran, China, and Cuba, requesting the convening of an urgent debate during the ongoing 61st session on the protection of children and educational institutions in international armed conflicts. the aerial attacks on Shajareh Tayyebeh Girls' School in Minab, Iran, as a grave breach of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. As decided by the Council during its 45th meeting on Wednesday, 25 March, we shall now proceed with this urgent debate. The urgent debate will follow the same format as a general debate. of this Human Rights Council and will follow the time-saving measures adopted by the Council on 9 February 2026. Speaking time will therefore be limited to one minute and 30 seconds for everyone. The list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I now give the floor to Mr. Volker Turk, the High Commissioner for Human Rights, for his statement by video. He has the floor.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the bombing of Sharjere Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab evoked a visceral horror. The images of bombed-out classrooms and grieving parents showed clearly who pays the highest price for war, civilians with no power in the decisions that led to conflict. In this case, I reported 168 pupils, teachers, school staff, and their loved ones. I send my deepest condolences to the bereaved families. Whatever differences countries have, we can all agree they will not be solved by killing school children. That is why we have the laws of war to protect children and other civilians caught up in conflict as well as schools and all civilian infrastructure. In the case of this school, the onus is on those who carried out the attack to investigate it promptly, impartially, transparently, and thoroughly to determine the facts and lay the basis for accountability. Senior US officials have said the strike is under investigation. I call for that process to be concluded as soon as possible and for its findings to be made public. There must be justice for the terrible harm done. It is gravely concerning that around the world, attacks on schools are increasing. In 2024, such attacks surged by a shocking 44%, leaving 52 million children out of the classroom. I call on all countries to take urgent steps to protect educational facilities and those who study and work in them. Mr. President, resort to the use of force at a time when negotiations were ongoing is a strategic failure that has had a devastating impact on civilians. Bombs and missiles are not the path to a sustainable peace. They bring death, destruction, and misery, in many cases only deepening grievances and fueling future violence. In Iran, as the conflict has progressed, US and Israeli attacks have increasingly struck densely populated residential areas and destroyed civilian infrastructure. Homes, medical facilities, schools, courts, transport networks, and energy installations have been hit across all 31 provinces of the country. According to the Iranian authorities, more than 1,900 civilians have been killed and tens of thousands injured. The targeting of nuclear facilities is reckless beyond comprehension. These attacks raise serious concerns over compliance with international humanitarian and human rights law under which the protection of civilians must remain central. Mr. President, the people of Iran are caught between conflict and repression. I'm gravely concerned by reports that since the start of the hostilities, the Iranian authorities have intensified their crackdown on civic space. Law enforcement authorities have repeatedly said that dissent will be treated as collaboration with the enemy and punished harshly for acts including filming damaged sites or communicating about the conflict. The authorities have intensified arrests, judicial cases, and bans against people and media outlets accused of promoting so-called enemy narratives. We have reason to believe hundreds of people have been arrested while journalists, activists, and public figures have been placed under surveillance. The internet has been shut down for nearly a month. War does not reduce the responsibility of the Iranian authorities to abide by their human rights obligations. Mr. President, the military escalation in the Middle East and the Gulf is reaching dangerous levels. It must end. There is a high and rising risk of further contagion and increased civilian suffering in the countries directly involved. Beyond the region, there are fears of grave economic consequences from deepening poverty and hunger to shortages of medicine and fuel. It is imperative that all parties halt the escalation. I call on the United States and Israel to end their attacks against Iran, and I call on Iran to stop attacking its neighbors and to respect and protect the human rights of its own people. I urge restraint on all sides and implore the parties to conflict to return to negotiations, the only path towards a durable solution to their differences. Divisions within this council must not distract us from a shared focus on the human rights of people across the Gulf and the Middle East. As I address you for a second time in three days, I urge all states to prioritize preventing further suffering, protecting all civilians regardless of nationality or location, and seeking long-term sustainable peace. Thank you.

I thank the High Commissioner. And I now give the floor to Ms. Farida Shaheed, the Special Rapporteur on the Right to Education, who will deliver a statement on behalf of the Coordination Committee of special procedures by video. She has the floor.

Mr. President, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates, today I address you in my capacity as a special rapporteur on the right to education and on behalf of the Special Procedures Coordination Committee. The Special Procedures have been closely monitoring the rapid escalation of hostilities during the military offensive of the United States of America and Israel against Iran. In our statement earlier this month, we strongly condemned the strike on the elementary school in Minhar. On 28 February, U.S. Tomahawk missiles struck the elementary school. 45 a.m. local time as classes were underway. At least 175 people were killed, mostly children aged 7 to 12. Large parts of the schools were reduced to rubble, families torn apart and devastated. I reiterate what we said in our statement. A strike on a school is a grave assault on children, on education, and the future of an entire community. International humanitarian law is crystal clear. Attacks directed against civilians or civilian objects, or which fail to adequately distinguish between military objectives and civilian infrastructure, constitute serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. This is not an isolated incident. According to various reports, over 600 schools and educational facilities have already been destroyed or severely damaged, and over 230 children and teachers killed. The strike on the school is just one consequence of this war. Over 1,000 civilians have been killed, 3 million people displaced, hospitals and World Heritage sites destroyed in Iran, while striking oil infrastructure risks serious long-term health effects in the region. As parents, we watch them grow with tears and fears and sleepless nights and sheer joy when they learn and laugh, discover and grow. There's no bigger pain for any parent than to lose a child, an unimaginable rupture of life. Excellencies, on behalf of all the world's parents, I ask who exactly will be held responsible for these deaths? Surely we cannot allow the lives of these and other children to be extinguished without consequences. Mr. President, schools are civilian objects, and children are expressly protected under international humanitarian law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Directing attacks against civilian objects, unless they become military objects, is prohibited under treaty and customary international humanitarian law. Indiscriminate attacks are strictly prohibited. Intentional attacks on educational buildings that are not military objectives are war crimes listed in the Rome Statute under Article 8. But what does this really mean in terms of liability? Ultimately, the responsibility lies with the state that carried out the attack on the school to conduct thorough, prompt, and impartial investigations into this attack and all attacks on civilian objects. Preliminary investigation by the US military has concluded that American forces were responsible for the missile strike. The school and other buildings in the compound were each struck individually by precision munition, meaning that U.S. military clearly intended to strike the school. Ongoing investigation suggests that the school attack might have been a result of a mistaken targeting by the U.S. military using outdated intelligence. If officially confirmed, this would mean that the principle of taking feasible precautions in attacks was most likely violated. In particular, the rule that a party to the conflict must do everything feasible to verify that targets pursued are in fact military objectives. If journalists and civil society groups using only open source access could relatively quickly establish that the school was separated from the wider compound and visibly marked. The US military, with all the tools at its disposal, surely could have done so prior to the attack. They had an obligation to do so. The question is why outdated information was used. Who failed to verify the data? Who exactly in the chain of command was responsible for verification, and what liability under domestic and international law will the person or persons face in the end. The families of the victims deserve a transparent and authoritative account of what happened, as well as justice and accountability. Mr. President, we mandate holders, appointed by the Human Rights Council, stress the importance of accountability. All violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law must be investigated and those responsible held to account. We welcome the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran regarding ongoing violations, including the attack on the Minab school. It's vital that the fact-finding mission carry out its mandate fully without obstruction. We also welcome the Secretary-General's annual report on children and armed conflict as a form of accountability, since its annex lists parties to conflict which have attacked schools, which are considered one of six grave violations against children. State responsibility in the form of reparation, restitution, and rehabilitation for internationally wrongful acts is another important channel. This may include rebuilding schools, trauma-informed education, and supporting the reintegration of affected children into education. By 2025, the report on the right to education in armed conflict argues that education itself can be a form of reparation for children who survive the horrors of war. Excellencies, this tragic incident must not fall into an accountability gap. Every possible avenue for accountability must be explored. And if the existing framework falls short of holding the responsible party to account, the priority must be creating a stronger framework. This is a matter of justice. Parents and children around the world need assurance that such violations will not be repeated. There must be no impunity for countries and decision makers who permit attacks on children. In concluding, I stress that the right to education remains fully applicable during armed conflict, protected under both international human rights law and international humanitarian law, which have mutually reinforcing and complementary roles. The right to education is a life-saving right. In crisis, education gives children a supportive environment, a sense of normalcy, psychosocial support, and pathways to recovery. Protecting education is both a legal obligation and investment in peace. Therefore, education must be treated as a core humanitarian priority alongside food, water, shelter, and healthcare. While this urgent debate focuses on the school attack in Minh Ha, The human cost of this conflict extends across the region. The protection of all civilians on all sides of this conflict must remain the central priority. All efforts must be directed towards preventing further harm, ensuring access to essential services, and safeguarding the dignity and rights of all affected populations. The world needs peaceful coexistence where communities can live without fear and children grow up safely. We call for an immediate end to hostilities and urge all parties to fully respect their obligations under international humanitarian law to protect civilians and to provide justice and effective redress for victims. The special procedures stand ready to support the Council and all relevant actors in addressing the human rights implications of this crisis promoting accountability, and advancing efforts towards de-escalation and lasting peace. Finally, our thoughts are with the families of the victims and the survivors who now face unimaginable trauma. The killing of children can never, ever be justified. Thank you.

I thank the Special Rapporteur on the Right to Education, who spoke on behalf of the Coordination Committee of Special Procedures, and I would like to remind the special procedures that the Council has affected the time-saving measures on 9 February 2026 to remind them of time limits when speaking before the Council as everybody else. I now give the floor to Ms. Mohadesse Falahe, mother of two children killed in the strike on the school in Meenup.

President, ladies and gentlemen, I'm a mother. A mother who even now, when passing by my kids' room, feels the urge to open the door and see them sleeping in their beds, as always, or sitting there drawing. But the room is silent, much more silent than any home should ever be. That morning was like any other. It was routine for me to straighten their shoes by the door, comb their hair and put their backpacks on their shoulders. There was no sign that this would be the last time. As they walked out the door, they simply said, "Mum, come pick us up after school." That simple sentence now repeats in my mind a thousand times, and each time my heart burns with pain. No mother ever thinks she will send her child off to school with a smile, only to be met with silence. No mother is prepared to hear the words, "Your child is not coming back." These days, whenever I see any child for a moment, I think, "Maybe." Maybe if it were my kids, Mahdiye and Mayamine, he or she would be running just like that, laughing just like that, living just like that. The clothes I bought with such joy for the New Year and Nowruz are still there, their notebooks left unfinished, and their dreams, dreams they never had the chance to continue writing. I'm not just a grieving mother, no. I am the voice of all the mothers who sent their children to school believing they would be safe. A school was meant to be a place for learning, laughing and building the future, a safe place for the children who were supposed to build the future of this world, not a place where their future is extinguished in an instant. I call upon the Human Rights Council and its members upon the responsible institutions and upon all those who have the ability and the duty to defend the lives of children, not to let this tragedy be forgotten. The truth must be brought to light, and Israel and the United States, who are the cause of this suffering, must be held accountable, not for revenge, but for justice, so that the world knows that children's lives are not worthless and that no parent should ever again have to endure such a weight. Thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Saeed Abbas Arakchi, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Bismillahir Rahmanir Raheem, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues, Iran stands today amid the throes of an illegal war imposed by two bullying nuclear-armed regimes, the United States and Israel. This war of aggression is blatantly unjustified and brutal. They initiated this aggression on 28 February, while Iran and the United States were engaged in a diplomatic process to resolve America's alleged concerns over Iran's nuclear program. They betrayed diplomacy for a second time in the course of nine months by torpedoing the negotiating table. Among the most harrowing manifestations of this aggression was the calculated, phased assault on Shajarat Hayyabeh Elementary School in the city of Minab, south of Iran, where more than 175 students and teachers were slaughtered in cold blood. This barbaric attack is but the visible tip of a far bigger iceberg, one that conceals beneath its surface far graver catastrophes, namely the normalization of the most abhorrent violations of human rights and humanitarian law, and the audacity to commit atrocity crimes with impunity. Mr. President, at a time when the American-Israeli aggressors, in their own assertions, possess the most advanced technologies and the highest precision military and data systems, no one can believe that the attack on this school was anything other than deliberate and intentional. Targeting Shajara Tayyiba school was a war crime and a crime against humanity, one that demands unequivocal condemnation by all. and unambiguous accountability for the culprits. This atrocity cannot be justified, cannot be concealed, and must not be met with silence and indifference. The attack on Shajar al-Tajribah School in Minab was not a mere incident nor a miscalculation. The United States' contradictory remarks aimed at justifying their crime could not, in any manner, elude their responsibility. To denounce such a merciless assault on a place inherently civilian, a place where the most innocents reside and pursue knowledge, is not merely a legal obligation under human rights frameworks. It is a moral and human imperative. Our conscience will judge us more profoundly than any tribunal ever could. Distinguished delegates, Shajarat Hayeb Elementary School has not been the only casualty of American-Israeli atrocity crimes during the past 27 days of their illegal war. Human rights and international humanitarian law have been massively and systematically violated by the invaders in an unprecedentedly brutal manner. They are targeting civilians and civilian infrastructures with no regard for laws of war and basic principles of humanity and civility. More than 600 schools have been demolished or damaged. across Iran, and more than 1,000 students and teachers martyred or wounded as the result. The aggressors, who are arrogantly shouting, "No mercy, no quarters," and threatening to strike Iran's vital infrastructure, have been attacking hospitals, ambulances, health workers, Red Crescent rescuers, refineries, water sources, and residential areas. War crime and crime against humanity are not sufficiently describing the gravity of the atrocities they are committing. The aggressors' targeting pattern, accompanied by their rhetoric, leave little doubt as to their clear intent to commit genocide. Distinguished colleagues, this unjust war of whims by the United States and Israel against the noble nation of Iran is the direct result of silence in the face of earlier manifestations of lawlessness and atrocity in occupied Palestine, Lebanon, and elsewhere. Indifference and silence in the face of injustices would bring no security and peace. It would invite more insecurity and rights violations. The United Nations and the core values it embodies as well as the overall human rights framework, are at serious stake. You all need to call out the aggressors and let them know that the community of states, the human collective conscience, hold them accountable for the abhorrent crimes they are committing against Iranians. Iran has never sought war. Iranians are a peaceful, noble nation inheriting one of the richest civilizations on Earth. Yet, they have demonstrated absolute resolve and determination to defend themselves against the brutal aggressors who know no boundary in perpetrating all sorts of crimes, a defence that shall persist as long as needed. And thank you for your attention.

Thank you. Before we proceed with the list of speakers, Allow me to request to all delegations to deal with human rights issues with dignity, and also remind all of you to adhere to the well-established principles of the United Nations, and this includes to uphold UN standards when referring to countries. The list of speakers is now closed. And we shall now begin with the list of members of the Council, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Norway on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of Iceland and Norway, we welcome this urgent debate. The Middle East is on fire. Human suffering is severe and immediate. Beyond the region, it has growing and profound consequences on global stability, on energy and food security. We are deeply alarmed by the human rights and humanitarian crisis caused by the warfare, with civilians displaced, injured and killed across the region. On the first day of the war, more than 170 children were deplorably killed when a girls' school in Minab was hit. And since then, several schools, hospitals, energy infrastructure and other civilian objects have also been hit, increasing risks to all civilians. This is unacceptable.

We call on all.

Parties to respect IHL and to use the tools of the Safe Schools Declaration to protect children and education. Neither the US and Israeli strikes against Iran, nor the Iranian attacks on countries in the region, are in accordance with international law. The human rights situation in Iran, especially with regards to women and girls, is intolerable. Once again, we call on the Islamic Republic of Iran to respect all human rights for all. President, we call on the parties to end the war and to find diplomatic solutions to unlock the current stalemate in the region.

Thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Mr. President, I speak on behalf of the EU. Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Liechtenstein, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine align themselves with this statement. The EU deplores the loss of all civilian life and calls for an immediate end to strikes against civilian infrastructure. We call for de-escalation and restraint, protection of civilians, and respect of international law, including the UN Charter, by all parties. We are deeply saddened by the loss of children's lives in Iran, including those killed in the strike against the school in Minab. The EU calls on all parties to take all measures to ensure children's rights are fully respected. Attacks against civilian objects constitute a violation of IHL. We call on all parties to take necessary measures to protect children, including ensuring that civilian facilities are not attacked. The EU calls on Iran to cease violence and repression against its own people. The EU calls for the respect of the rights and freedoms of the Iranian people. The EU has taken targeted restrictive measures against those responsible for serious human rights violations in Iran and will continue to do so as long as necessary. The EU fully supports the work of the FFM and of the Sr. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Venezuela on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, President. The Group of Friends in Defence of the United Nations Charter welcomes this initiative of Iran, China and Cuba to hold an urgent debate. We vehemently condemn the killing of 168 children at Mina Primary School in the Islamic Republic of Iran on 28 February. The United States and Israel must respect international humanitarian law and international human rights law. We are deeply worried at the attack on Minna Primary School, which led to the deaths of nearly 170 children, and many more were injured. Attacks on schools are war crimes. All states have the basic responsibility to protect children, ensure full enjoyment of human rights, and to uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law in the context of armed conflict. We're deeply worried at the growing threats to civilian infrastructure as well as the environmental impacts of acid rain and the poisoning which results from attacks on oil infrastructure. The long-term consequences of these acts will go beyond the current generations. We call for distinction, proportionality, and precaution to be fully respected during hostilities. Thank you very much.
Thank you. And I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Indonesia strongly condemns the deliberate attack against the Saja Resti Habibie Girls School in Minab. carried out in the context of the unprovoked military campaign by the US and Israel across Iran. We extend our deepest condolences to the people of Iran, particularly the families of the victims. Across the Middle East, we have seen thousands of schools in Gaza, Iran, and Lebanon, along with hospitals and homes have been destroyed in patterns of this attack. No military or political justification can excuse the killing of children. This attack reflects a method of warfare we have seen in Gaza. Repeated strikes on civilian infrastructure where harm to civilians is part of a broader pattern, resulting in widespread destruction. This Council has to recognize the growing application of the Israel-Gaza method, where children and families are assassinated for political and military purposes. Francesca Albanese clearly warned us about this. I call on this Council to recognize this danger. The growing grave violation of international humanitarian and human rights law may amount to war crimes in Iran and across the region. Accountability is essential, and this Council must not allow silence or selectivity to embolden impunity. Indonesia therefore calls for an independent and impartial investigation, full accountability for those responsible, and comprehensive redress for victims.
Thank you. Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Mr. President, Ethiopia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter. including the prohibition of the use of force and the peaceful resolution of disputes. We express our grave concern over the deteriorating situation in the Middle East and urgently call for an immediate cessation of hostilities.

We extend our condolences to the families.

Of the victims and to all those affected by the ongoing violence in the region. We urge all parties to exercise maximum restraint. take all feasible measures to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and fully comply with international humanitarian and human rights law. Ethiopia calls upon the international community to redouble its efforts towards de-escalation and to place renewed emphasis on dialogue and diplomacy as the only viable path to sustainable peace and lasting stability. In closing, Ethiopia remains ready to constructively engage with and support all credible initiatives aimed at advancing peace, strengthening security, and fostering stability.

I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Thank you, President. Children are most vulnerable victims, and they're the ones that we should particularly protect during armed conflict. Humanity should spare no effort to guarantee the future of our planet. All parties to armed conflicts must understand that if they do not do this, then they are crossing unforgivable red lines. Colombia vehemently... condemns the attack on Minab Primary School, which took the lives of nearly 200 girls. And we offer our solidarity to all the victims of hostilities in the Middle East. And we deeply regret the fact that hundreds of civilians have suffered the consequences of the escalation of violence arising from the military aggression of the United States and Israel against Iran. As the High Commissioner Special Rapporteur for Iran and the International Investigation Mission for Iran have mentioned, all parties to conflict must respect the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution and respect the protection that they must provide under international humanitarian law to schools and education and apply the guidelines for preventing the military use of schools and universities during armed conflicts. We must ensure that this kind of tragedy is not repeated and that these facts do not go unpunished and those held accountable be brought to book. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you, President. We'd like to thank the sponsoring countries for having convened this debate. Mexico shares the deep concern at the widespread impact on human rights resulting from the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, which began on the 28th of February. Mexico offers its solidarity to all affected governments and peoples, and we deeply regret the humanitarian impact of this conflict, which is affecting the most vulnerable people, particularly girls, who suffer a differentiated impact because of factors such as gender and age. We particularly deplore attacks against schools, such as the attack on Minab school, as well as against hospitals and basic civilian infrastructure, which are tantamount to flagrant violations of international humanitarian law. The loss of young lives in armed conflict is an unacceptable tragedy and a violation of their fundamental rights, including their right to life. The Geneva Conventions call for protection of civilians and to distinguish between military and civilian objects, including schools. So, we urge all parties to enter into dialogue and find a peaceful solution to this dispute and respect international humanitarian law and international human rights law. This is the only way to put a stop to this conflict. Thank you very much, President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Mr. President, the attack on the Sharajeh Tajyebeh Girls' School in Minab, Iran, which claimed the lives of 168 innocent girls, It's a breach of the bottom line of human morality, the most egregious violation of human rights, and a blatant contempt for IHL. China is deeply shocked by the attack. We strongly condemn it and express our sympathies for the families of the victims. The US and Israel launched the attack on Iran without the authorization of the Security Council, which is the root cause of this tragedy. The U.S. and Israel killed Iran's leaders, seriously violated the human rights of the Iranian people, and triggered an escalation of conflicts in the Middle East, forcibly drawing regional countries into the situation. The sovereignty, security, and territorial integrity of all countries should be fully respected. China strongly condemns all acts that violate international law and indiscriminately target civilians and non-military objectives. All hotspot issues should be resolved through dialogue and negotiation, not through the use of force. All parties must seize every opportunity for peace, launch the peace process in good faith, take practical actions to protect the basic human rights of the people in the region, and safeguard peace and stability in the Middle East. Thank you, President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

Thank you, Mr. President. India remains deeply concerned at the evolving situation in West Asia. As a proximate neighbor with critical stakes in the security and stability of the region, these developments evoke great anxiety. India expresses profound grief over the loss of precious lives due to the attack on the Sharji Tahiyyah Girls School in Manab. This tragedy underlines once again the urgent need to ensure that schools, hospitals, energy and other civilian infrastructure are never targets in situations of armed conflict. India reiterates that there is no alternative to dialogue and diplomacy. India has consistently urged all sides to exercise restraint, avoid escalation and prioritize the safety of civilians. All outstanding issues must be addressed through peaceful means. with full respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states. Mr. President, India stands ready to support all constructive efforts aimed at de-escalation, fostering dialogue, and promoting lasting peace, stability, and security in West Asia.

Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iraq.

Shikarnis. Thank you, Mr. President. This urgent debate takes place in a serious context because of the escalation of military operations that affected Iraq, the region, and the world in a direct threat of stability and security and a flagrant violation of the basic principles and norms of international law. This puts at risk the economic interests and the civility of civilians. We strongly condemn any attack against children, educational institutions, and education institutions in armed conflicts because this is a flagrant violation of the principles of IHL and international human rights law. Targeting schools is also a flagrant violation of human rights and a direct threat to the future and stability of communities. Iraq reiterates that the protection of children in armed conflicts is the common and responsibility of the international community. We reiterate our call for the respect of the rights of children at all times, preserving their dignity and rights. We reiterate that the expansion of war would deepen crises, undermine stability, and we call for dialogue as a way to peacefully resolve differences and achieve peace and stability. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you, Mr. President. As consistently underlined throughout this Human Rights Council session, Slovenia condemns the military escalation by all parties in the Middle East. This war is fueling dangerous regional instability, profound human suffering, and destruction. Numerous young lives have deplorably been lost, the girls' lives at the school in Minab, as well as in other parts of the region. International humanitarian law is clear. Attacks on schools are prohibited. The Geneva Conventions and their additional protocols impose obligations to afford special protection to children. The Convention on the Rights of the Child reinforces the right to education, even during conflict. Within the children and armed conflict framework, attacks against schools and hospitals are recognized as one of the six grave violations against children. Despite these clear norms, deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of schools, educational facilities, teachers, and students are increasing in both frequency and scale. Perpetrators of grave violations against children and against civilians in general must be brought to justice, in line with international law and standards. To conclude, Mr. President, Slovenia reiterates its call on all parties in this conflict for de-escalation, maximum restraint, and full respect of international law. Only diplomacy and negotiations in good faith are a viable path towards peace and security for children and civilians in the region. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Thank you, President. Spain endorses the EU statement on the 28th of February. The illegal bombing by Israel and the US has triggered another dangerous escalation of violence in the Middle East. There's also been unacceptable waves of attacks since then. We condemn all violations of international humanitarian law and the UN Charter. The pupils and teachers of Minab school were also the victims of a breach of international law. We hope that the fact-finding mission, the special rapporteur on the human rights in Iran, will shed light on who is accountable. Spain is committed to justice and transparency. We shouldn't trivialise the killing of children through bombings as mere collateral damage of conflicts. When you destroy a school, you destroy the future of a generation. That's why Spain firmly believes in the Safe Schools Declaration, which is signed. But we must be coherent. Whilst Iran has convened this urgent debate, the authorities in that country are carrying out summary killings and repress their people because they want to freely express themselves and demonstrate. And Masha Amini is just an example of the particular victimization of girls and women. Spain calls for everyone to respect international law and a return to diplomacy, above all, to avoid future atrocities. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Brazil strongly condemns the bombing of the education facility in Minab that resulted in the deaths of 168 schoolgirls aged between 7 and 12, along with their educators. This act constitutes a grave violation of human rights and humanitarian law. We are currently witnessing an erosion of multilateralism. alongside systematic disregard for international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law. This appears to have become a constant across various global conflicts. The current situation in the Middle East would justify a comprehensive and non-selective debate in this Council, Mr. President, one that addresses human rights violations in the entire region and the responsibilities of all parties involved in the hostilities. It would also demand the fulfilment of international obligations to protect civilians, and we regret that the path of fragmentation has prevailed over a holistic approach to the crisis. We recall that the protection of children in armed conflict will be the subject of a specific resolution during this 61st session, presented by Gruluck and the European Union. To conclude, let me be clear, children must be protected at all times, and without exception. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Thank you, President. President, the war in the Middle East is a serious threat to security in the region and must be stopped forthwith. It's only by respecting international law and returning to diplomacy that we will ensure that there is lasting stability and security in the region. The bombing of the Minab school led to an outpouring of emotion. France offers its condolences to the families of the victims, and we hope that those accountable will be held to account for this tragedy. We call for respect by all parties to international humanitarian law. It's vital to swiftly put a stop to the targeting of civilian infrastructure in order to protect civilians and ensure access to basic services such as energy production.
